observed_forms: at a loss as to + how/what/why

senses.definition: Unsure what to say or do.
senses.example: I was at a loss as to how to explain the unexpected result.

synonyms.note: about what to do or say

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: be at a loss; be at a loss for words; be at a loss as to + what/how/why-clause. At a loss for words specifically means unable to think of something to say: I was at a loss for words when I heard the news.

classification_reason: One idiom: be at a loss; be at a loss for words; be at a loss as to what/how/why. The X-marked variants are supporting content, not additional notes.

senses.definition: Surprise someone when they are unprepared.
senses.example: The follow-up question caught me off guard.
senses.usage_note: Common patterns: catch + person + off guard; be caught off guard. Passive: We were caught off guard by the sudden change. Being put on the spot emphasizes pressure to respond, which need not involve surprise.

classification_reason: Be surprised and unprepared; keep distinct from being required to answer publicly.

senses.definition: Make someone answer or act immediately in a difficult or embarrassing situation.
senses.example: Asking her to defend the estimate without warning put her on the spot.

synonyms.note: broader; does not specifically require an immediate response

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: put + person + on the spot; be put on the spot. Passive: I was put on the spot during the meeting. This emphasizes pressure to respond; catch someone off guard emphasizes surprise and lack of preparation.

classification_reason: Require an immediate answer or decision, often under social pressure. This can happen without surprise; it is not the same meaning as catch off guard.

senses.definition: Accumulate into a growing amount.
senses.example: My unfinished tasks have piled up.
senses.usage_note: Common patterns: tasks/emails pile up; have piled up; have been piling up; pile up + things. Different forms, same expression: When tasks pile up, I get overwhelmed. / My work has been piling up all week.

senses.definition: Put things together in a pile.
senses.example: We piled up the empty boxes by the door.

synonyms.note: usually suggests a more orderly arrangement

classification_reason: One phrasal verb: accumulate; include Tasks pile up / have piled up / have been piling up. The later X-marked repetition is not a veto on the explicitly retained earlier entry.

senses.definition: Throughout the relevant period, often understood or revealed later.
senses.example: The answer was in the documentation all along.
senses.usage_note: Common patterns: know/suspect something all along; be there all along; usually placed near the end of the clause. Not restricted to one tense: I knew something was wrong all along. It often appears near the end of the clause.

classification_reason: Throughout the relevant period, often with a later realization. It works with different tenses; it is not a present-perfect-continuous-only grammar frame.

term: off the top of one's head
tts_text: off the top of my head
observed_forms: off the top of one's head
off the top of my head

senses.definition: From memory, without checking or preparing.

synonyms.note: does not always imply an unprepared answer

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: off the top of my/your head; off the top of my head, + clause. Change the possessive: Can you name a few examples off the top of your head?

classification_reason: A useful lexical meaning or fixed expression with no equivalent dedicated note found in the current sources.

observed_forms: I can't find the right words

senses.definition: Express a thought or feeling in spoken or written language.

classification_reason: Express a thought or feeling verbally. Keep I cannot find the right words as a related example/near paraphrase, not a second target or a purported literal instance of put.

senses.definition: Move with small, repeated twists of the body or a body part.

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: wriggle out of + place/clothing; wriggle free. Writhe often describes twisting because of pain or distress; wriggle does not require pain.

classification_reason: Small repeated twisting movements; distinct from existing writhe, which commonly describes pain or distress. Lower priority for production.

senses.definition: Twist, or cause something to twist, into an unusual or strained shape.

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: contort your body/face; be contorted with pain. The shape or strain matters; movement need not be repeated. Her face was contorted with pain.

classification_reason: Twist into a strained or unusual shape; not a duplicate of writhe. Recognition is sufficient for now.

senses.definition: Wash something briefly with liquid, often to remove soap or small particles.

synonyms.note: broader; may involve soap or a more thorough cleaning

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: rinse your mouth with + liquid; rinse + object; rinse something out/off. Also: Rinse the cup out. / Rinse the soap off your hands. Gargling moves liquid around the back of the throat; rinsing your mouth does not require that.

senses.definition: A brief wash with liquid.

classification_reason: Wash something briefly with liquid; include rinse your mouth with water, rinse a cup, rinse something out. Not the same action as gargling.

senses.definition: Move liquid around the back of your throat while breathing out, making a bubbling sound.

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: gargle with + liquid; gargle with warm salt water. Rinsing your mouth washes the mouth; gargling specifically involves the back of the throat.

classification_reason: Move liquid around the back of the throat, often making a sound; gargle with warm salt water. Keep separate from rinse unless a full two-term contrast is later chosen.

senses.definition: Sheets, blankets, or other bedding used to cover a person in bed.

senses.definition: Forgetful or inattentive because your thoughts are elsewhere.

senses.definition: Friendly and pleasant; for joking or competition, without hostile intent.
senses.example: There is a good-natured rivalry between our teams.
senses.usage_note: Common patterns: good-natured rivalry/teasing; a good-natured exchange. Also: There was some good-natured teasing during lunch.

classification_reason: One adjective demonstrated by good-natured rivalry and good-natured teasing. The X-marked person example need not be retained. Rivalry remains a separate noun, not another sense of good-natured.

senses.definition: An ongoing competitive relationship between people, groups, or organizations.
senses.example: There is a long-standing rivalry between the two clubs.

synonyms.note: broader; need not describe an ongoing relationship

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: a rivalry between A and B; rivalry with + competitor; a friendly/long-standing rivalry. A rivalry can be friendly or hostile. Rivalry between A and B; rivalry with a competitor.

classification_reason: Ongoing competition: a rivalry between A and B; rivalry with a competitor. Good-natured is one possible modifier, not part of the noun's fixed identity.

senses.definition: Designed to be very hard to misuse or get wrong.
senses.example: We need a foolproof way to avoid accidental deployments.

synonyms.note: broader; does not specifically emphasize resistance to mistakes

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: a foolproof method/plan/system; make + process/instructions + foolproof. Also: We should make the installation process foolproof. It often expresses strong confidence, not a literal guarantee that failure is impossible.

classification_reason: One adjective: a foolproof method; make the process foolproof. The make + object + adjective grammar already exists; the new learning is the adjective.

senses.definition: Make someone learn or remember something through repeated, insistent instruction.
senses.example: My teacher drilled that rule into us.

synonyms.note: can describe a slower or less repetitive process

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: drill + rule/idea/lesson + into + person. Can sound forceful. A pronunciation drill is a practice exercise, not this instruction idiom.

classification_reason: Teach something through insistent repetition; can sound forceful. Not the same sense as pronunciation drill, which the learner crossed out.

senses.definition: use one thing instead of another.

senses.usage_note: Common patterns: substitute NEW for OLD; replace OLD with NEW; substitute for someone; a substitute for + noun. Same replacement, opposite order: We substituted a local database for the cloud service. / We replaced the cloud service with a local database. NEW is what you use; OLD is what it replaces.

senses.definition: someone or something used instead of another.
senses.example: Oat milk is a substitute for regular milk.

term: compromise / meet halfway / concede / give in / back down
pronunciation:
compromise: /ˈkɑmprəmaɪz/
meet halfway: /mit ˌhæfˈweɪ/
concede: /kənˈsid/
give in: /ɡɪv ˈɪn/
back down: /bæk ˈdaʊn/
tts_text: compromise. meet halfway. concede. give in. back down
observed_forms: compromise / meet halfway / concede / give in / back down

senses.definition: an agreement reached by accepting less than originally wanted.
senses.example: We reached a compromise on the deadline.

senses.common_patterns: reach a compromise; compromise with someone on something; compromise security

situations.examples: “We compromised on the deadline.” / “We met each other halfway on the deadline.”

situations.guidance: Concede can mean yield something after resisting.

situations.examples: “I concede that your approach is simpler.”
situations.guidance: Concede that + clause means admit a point; it need not mean accept a demand.

situations.examples: “She finally gave in.” / “She finally backed down.”
situations.guidance: Often overlapping; neither requires a mutual compromise.

situations.situation: An action puts something at risk.
situations.guidance: Compromise also means weaken or endanger.

comparison.note: Compromise and meet someone halfway often describe the same mutual adjustment. Concede can mean admit a point or yield something. Give in and back down often overlap for stopping resistance; neither requires both sides to adjust. Compromise security means put security at risk, not negotiate.

senses.definition: accept less than originally wanted to reach agreement.
senses.example: We compromised on the deadline.

senses.definition: weaken or put something at risk.
senses.example: Sharing passwords can compromise security.

senses.definition: Accept part of another person's wishes so both sides can agree.
senses.example: If you can extend the deadline, I'll meet you halfway on the scope.

senses.common_patterns: meet someone halfway; meet each other halfway

senses.definition: Admit that something is true, or yield something after resisting.
senses.example: I concede that your approach is simpler.

senses.common_patterns: concede that + clause; concede a point; concede defeat; make a concession (the related noun phrase). We made a concession on the deadline to reach an agreement. A concession is something you agree to give up or allow; it need not mean that both sides compromise.

senses.definition: Stop resisting and agree to a demand or temptation.
senses.example: I finally gave in and agreed to help.

senses.definition: Withdraw a position or demand after opposition.
senses.example: She refused to back down on the deadline.

senses.common_patterns: back down on/from + position/demand; refuse to back down
